summary: Bloomberg interview, December 2018: Druckenmiller argues the Fed should pause hikes and QT because stock-market internals (cyclicals vs defensives), the yield curve, credit spreads and falling M2 growth are amber warning signals. Discusses QE-driven bubbles, Fed forward guidance, his long Treasury, short financials/credit and long cloud-growth positioning, the degraded price signals from algos, and shrinking hedge-fund alpha.

coverage.note: history of QE criticism, 2003 and 2007 Fed mistakes, corporate debt build, bond vigilantes, coincident vs leading indicators
stock-market internals, yield curve, credit leading economy, CDS and leveraged loans
gradual deleveraging, risk-reward of Fed pause, QT, Fed hiking reaction function
rate of change of conditions, QT and M2 liquidity, forward guidance
Fed mandate and lagging unemployment, QE suppressing volatility; Trump/Fed politics skipped
data dependence and changed conditions, autos/housing, central bank mistakes, trade war
unwinding liquidity, expected returns, global bear market, shorts in bears, Treasuries, QT timing
long Treasuries, secular growth/cloud stocks vs cyclicals, multiple compression, October losses
relative performance of growth vs cyclicals, tech disruptor pair, short financials, credit shorts
commodities and disinflation, politics and forecasting, Brexit pound payoff, markets as signal
algos degrade price signals, price vs news, short-term noise vs medium-term message, Trump election example
volatility needs trend, market efficiency and hedge fund alpha capacity
grumpy aside; investor qualities, emotional control, algo awareness

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: I became very concerned particularly when they started QE 3 that we hadn't learned our lessons from the past and we were going to create another yet another bubble in financial assets
claims.claim: QE pushes investors out the risk curve and creates asset bubbles whose bust leads to ever more radical monetary policy and weaker fiscal discipline.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: the only thing they ensured was a housing bubble
claims.claim: The Fed's 'considerable period' guidance in 2003 after growth had turned ensured only a housing bubble that led to the crisis; policy kept easy too long after the cycle turned.
claims.conditions: when the economy has already turned up

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: had he cut six to nine months earlier we would have had a recession but I don't know whether we've had a financial crisis
claims.claim: Counterfactual: if the Fed had cut and reversed policy 6-9 months earlier in 2007 when housing was clearly a disaster, there might have been a recession but not a financial crisis.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: corporate non-financial debt has grown from six trillion to nine point six trillion where I'm from that's about a 60% increase during that time corporate earnings increased 27%
claims.claim: Fed-driven risk-taking raised corporate debt 60% (from 6 to 9.6 trillion) while earnings rose only 27%; the borrowed money financed buybacks and M&A, a deflationary-bust setup.
claims.indicator: non-financial corporate debt vs earnings growth
claims.testable: yes - debt growth vs earnings growth

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: the bond market which would traditionally have been a vigilante from all this sort of behavior market signals were cancelled
claims.claim: QE and Fed behavior cancelled the bond-market vigilante signal, enabling more fiscal spending (Trump, Obama no entitlement cuts) and another bubble.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: if you look at the coincident economic indicators which I wish the Fed did they actually look at lagging indicators
claims.claim: Coincident indicators (GDP) look good, but the Fed relies on lagging ones; his own historical indicators are amber, not red.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: these cyclical elements of the economy particularly the front end sickles have show a completely different picture than the defensive parts
claims.claim: The inside of the stock market is the best economist: cyclicals (autos -30%, builders -35%, banks -25%, Russell 2000 -20%, retail -20%) are far weaker than defensives (utilities, staples, pharma up), so the S&P decline of 10-13% understates economic weakness; this set predicted the last four recessions.
claims.indicator: cyclical vs defensive sector relative performance, Russell 2000

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: the segment would be the yield curve again amber not red but we've inverted as you know from fives and to is just slightly
claims.claim: Yield curve flattening (2s5s slightly inverted, 2y 2.69, 5y 2.68, 10y 2.85) is an amber recession warning, made confusing by being a bull flattening at low rates while the market disbelieves the Fed's three to four hikes.
claims.conditions: especially when the market disbelieves Fed hike path

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: the other thing we've looked at historically is credit tends to lead the economy
claims.claim: Credit leads the economy; widening credit spreads signal trouble ahead.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: the GE CD s has gone from 50 basis points to 200 basis points since September first iBM
claims.claim: Corporate CDS are widening sharply (GE 50 to 200bp, IBM 30 to 80), high yield indexes are moving and leveraged loans are down 3%, a credit warning sign.
claims.indicator: single-name CDS, HY index, leveraged loans

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: the economy doesn't really care whether credit is in the banks or it's in the investment community
claims.claim: Because this cycle's bad credit sits in high-yield and leveraged loans rather than banks, there is no systemic financial crisis, but the economy is still hit by credit drying up.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: you want this bubble to unlined slowly now because if you don't and let's say these indicators turn red you may have to do a lot more crazy monetary stuff
claims.claim: Normalization should be slow because rapid tightening risks recession followed by more extreme easing, which would make eventual normalization harder.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: that cost to me is five to ten X
claims.claim: Risk-reward of the Fed pausing: if wrong, pausing costs little credibility, but hiking and shrinking the balance sheet by $50 billion a month with ECB not offsetting if the indicators are right costs five to ten times more.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: we're going to continue to hike until something either starts to break or financial conditions tighten
claims.claim: The Fed's reaction function is to keep hiking until something breaks or financial conditions tighten; market confusion arises because the Fed does not know the terminal rate.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: I would sneak one in every time I could under booming financial conditions and hopefully get to 3%
claims.claim: Hiking should be done when financial conditions are booming; hiking while the S&P is down 13%, cyclicals down 25-40% and the balance sheet is shrinking is not 'sneaking one in'.
claims.indicator: financial conditions at the time of hikes
claims.testable: partly - conditions at hike date vs outcomes

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: it's not even the level it's the rate of change
claims.claim: Markets react to the rate of change of tightening, and the US has not hiked into a market meltdown like this since Volcker (who had 12% inflation as justification).
claims.indicator: rate of change of rates / financial conditions
claims.testable: yes - change in financial conditions vs growth

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: need to raise money every month you know that creates government bonds selling every month and it tightens liquidity
claims.claim: QT tightens liquidity even if the Fed does not hike, because roll-off plus deficit financing means more government bonds sold into the market each month.
claims.indicator: Fed balance sheet roll-off, Treasury issuance
claims.testable: yes - net bond supply to private sector

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: m-2 growth has gone from about seven and a half percent to four percent over the last couple years it doesn't take a genius to figure out why liquidity is tightening
claims.claim: M2 growth falling from 7.5% to 4% shows liquidity tightening rapidly; money supply is a leading indicator few watch now.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: get out of the forward guidance business completely I don't know what it does other than tie their hands
claims.claim: Forward guidance ties the Fed's hands; after the taper tantrum they stuck to a QE and rate schedule to protect credibility even as conditions boomed, and now are stuck with wrong guidance.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: most recessions were preceded by a very low unemployment rate
claims.claim: Employment is a lagging indicator; most recessions start from very low unemployment, so the Fed should not use low unemployment as a reason to keep hiking.
claims.direction: recession risk up from very low unemployment
claims.testable: yes - unemployment level vs recession onset

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: since we went into the QE business and suppressed all this volatility
claims.claim: QE suppressed volatility, which made it harder for him to make money in bull and bear markets; the end of QE is when he expects volatility and opportunities to return.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: the SP was exploding up or an oil was $85 a barrel the reasons they got it in December have all changed
claims.claim: Credibility comes from being data dependent: when conditions that justified a December hike (S&P rising, oil $85) have reversed, policy should change.
claims.indicator: S&P, oil as inputs to Fed reaction

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: some of this leading stuff like autos and housing being this week with 2% rates has got to give them pause
claims.claim: Weak autos and housing at 2% rates are leading signs of malinvestment and debt drag on the economy.

claims.speaker: Eric (interviewer); confirmed by Druckenmiller
claims.quote: most of the really big money that you made at Duquesne was because of central bank mistakes and the consequent impact on market liquidity
claims.claim: Most of his large profits came from central bank mistakes and their effect on liquidity (confirmed 'correct').

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: we all know about smoot-hawley we know a way you all know about trade wars and we all know what all this nonsense is doing to business confidence
claims.claim: Trade wars hurt business confidence and growth; he had not foreseen this risk three years earlier.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: I could see the SP returning between 0 and 5 percent annually the next five years
claims.claim: After eight years of free money the S&P could return only 0-5% a year over five years (sideways or a big down), as unwinding liquidity is possible but difficult.
claims.testable: partly - cannot test with a single view

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: I think we're in a bear market in the sense that most stocks globally have been going down for nine to ten months
claims.claim: The global bear market is defined by most stocks falling for nine to ten months; the Dax and China peaked in January, showing economy-stock linkage.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: I went short the market in in July because I saw a cutie coming
claims.claim: He shorted in July on QT and lost money because he was three months early; thinking ahead in this market is costly.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: cutie I think is still set to accelerate the minute the ECB stops
claims.claim: Global QT should accelerate as the ECB stops, with global QT peaking October 1st; the price adjustment and de-risking could still give a favorable period over the next 16 months depending on central bank, Chinese and US government policy.
claims.indicator: global central bank balance sheet change
claims.testable: yes - net central bank asset change

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: it's always very difficult in a boom in a bear market they don't trade with rhythm you get these vicious rallies you get squeezed out of shorts
claims.claim: Shorting stocks in bear markets is hard because of vicious rallies and squeezes.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: I always made it in Treasuries because
claims.claim: In bear markets he made his money in Treasuries (e.g. the 2-year, 6.04% to 1.5-2% in 2000-01), because yields fall dramatically when the Fed eases.
claims.testable: yes - Treasury returns in equity bear markets

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: if the Fed makes a policy mistake it's not inconceivable to me at all that the two years back to fifty to sixty basis points
claims.claim: He is long 2-, 5- and 10-year Treasuries even at 2.68% because of the risk-reward; if the Fed errs, 2-year yields could fall to 50-60bp with QE and zero rates again.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: in a period of slow muted growth if you can find a 20 to 30 percent grower it's really like a long-term cashflow
claims.claim: In slow-growth environments, 20-30% growers behave like long-duration bonds, which supports secular growth stocks.
claims.testable: partly - growth factor vs macro regime

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: a lot of cyclical companies whose earnings grew at thirty percent
claims.claim: The tax cut and strong economy gave cyclical companies 30% earnings growth at 9x earnings versus growth names at 25-30x, interrupting the secular growth trend.
claims.indicator: cyclical vs growth earnings growth and multiples

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: you could argue that if we get in a mild recession demand for their product goes up because it's a way to cut costs
claims.claim: Cloud software (Microsoft, ServiceNow, Workday, Salesforce) is in the second inning of a shift; it grows regardless of macro and may benefit from mild recession as firms cut costs.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: these names have such data and when you go from nine times sales to seven times sales I even though your earnings aren't missing a beat it's a problem
claims.claim: High-multiple growth names suffer from multiple compression and high beta in sell-offs; he was 20-30% short the market in October yet lost 1% because these longs fell more.
claims.testable: yes - beta of growth stocks in drawdowns

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: all those names are 15 to 20 percent off their November lows whereas if you look at the banks and the cyclical z' they're all way low below they're November lows
claims.claim: Relative performance after the sell-off: cloud names recovered 15-20% off lows while banks and cyclicals stayed below their lows, which he reads as rational behavior.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: in tech we've been long the disruptors and short the disrupted which has worked
claims.claim: Long the disruptors and short the disrupted in tech worked well, but whipsaws in sell-offs when value buyers buy the disrupted at 10x earnings.
claims.conditions: fails when value buyers rotate in sharp sell-offs

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: why in the world would you buy a group that needs rates to go up to own it
claims.claim: He is short financials because banks need rates to go up to do well but equities do not do well when rates rise; if rates go down his cloud names should do better.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: the fact that AIG is down from 65 to 35
claims.claim: Credit-sensitive equities such as AIG (65 to 35), banks and Blackstone (-25% in a month) are warning lights that the market sees a problem in credit.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: it's easy to short credit for long Treasuries because again if rates are going up I don't want to be short credit
claims.claim: Pair short credit with long Treasuries: credit shorts profit when the economy falls apart (the same scenario in which Treasuries rally), but a credit short alone loses if rates rise.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: five or six percent absolute nominal yields for stuff that normally would be eight or nine an environment like this the risk award is just
claims.claim: High-yield at 5-6% absolute yield versus normal 8-9% gives terrible risk-reward in credit.
claims.testable: yes - HY yield vs long-run average

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: all the commodity indexes are down dramatically in the last four or five months and it's inconceivable that that doesn't float through
claims.claim: Falling oil and broad commodity indexes will pass through to lower inflation, which the Fed is ignoring.
claims.testable: yes - commodity price change vs CPI

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: I learned this business to solve economic puzzles and try and think 18 to 24 months ahead
claims.claim: Political risk is hard to forecast (the president thinks one or two days ahead), so his edge in economic puzzles is diluted; he expects the China dispute to be worked out but with low confidence.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: I could see the pound going to 135 if the markets
claims.claim: Brexit pound: upside to 1.35 if no hard break, downside through the post-referendum low of 1.18 if hard Brexit and Corbyn gains; payoff binary (+10% or -10%) unlike 1992.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: the beauty of the pound trade that you mentioned was a one-way bet it was either going to be flat or we're gonna make fifteen or twenty percent
claims.claim: He prefers asymmetric one-way bets over binary two-sided outcomes.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: no matter how powerful my thesis if they're screaming something else it's telling me
claims.claim: Take signals from markets: markets are smarter than he is, and if price disagrees with the thesis, reevaluate.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: the algos machines trading they tend to have different motivations like they're not nearly as momentum oriented
claims.claim: Since about 2012, algorithms (standard-deviation and data-driven models) and central bank signal-canceling have degraded the price-based trend signals he used to read; algos are less momentum-oriented.
claims.testable: yes - trend signal strength over time

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: if a company was reporting great earnings and everybody loved it and the stock just didn't act well for three or four months almost inevitably something happened that you didn't foresee
claims.claim: Price action versus news: when a stock fails to respond to good news the market is usually anticipating unseen bad news, and vice versa.
claims.testable: yes - post-earnings drift versus announcement reaction

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: the price signals that I learned how to read and how to listen to are broken
claims.claim: Short-horizon price reactions (e.g. Facebook earnings reaction reversed) no longer predict direction; over a week or two it is noise but over eight or nine months the market message is still good.
claims.testable: yes - signal quality at different horizons

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: the classic recent example was the night Trump was elected bonds got murdered
claims.claim: On the night of the election bonds and stocks opened sharply lower and cyclicals led, then reversed; the market anticipated recovery under Trump while pundits predicted Armageddon.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: Italy is only good if it's part of a trend and it's giving you entry points within a trend
claims.claim: Volatility only helps if it comes within a trend (entry points); volatility without trend creates whipsaws, where a volatility move may be mistaken for a trend start.
claims.testable: yes - trend-following performance in vol-without-trend regimes

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: the markets become more efficient it's become more difficult every time you buy something somebody's selling it to you
claims.claim: Competition from smarter participants has made markets more efficient and hedge fund alpha harder; only 10-20 discretionary funds will deserve 20% fees.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: there's still 3 trillion dollars of hedge fund money
claims.claim: Hedge funds ($3 trillion) chase a limited amount of alpha, which is too much capital.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: I think Bulls make more money than bears
claims.claim: Be skeptical but optimistic, since bulls make more money than bears over time.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: I've never made a buy at a low that I didn't just feel terrible and scared to death making it
claims.claim: Buying at lows feels terrible while selling at bottoms is easy, so investors need courage to fight emotions; the higher prices go the cheaper they look.

claims.speaker: Stanley Druckenmiller
claims.quote: you have to know if a particular price move is happening because of them or if it's happening for more natural causes
claims.claim: A trader needs to know what algos do, to tell whether a price move is algo-driven or fundamental.
